title: Traverse a binary tree — Inorder (Left → Root → Right gives sorted order in BST), Preorder (Root → Left → Right), Postorder (Left → Right → Root).
shortTitle: Traverse a Binary Tree (Inorder, Preorder, Postorder)

s1_definition.profdef: Traversing a binary tree means visiting every node exactly once in a defined order. The three depth-first traversals differ only in when the current node is visited relative to its subtrees. Inorder visits the left subtree, then the node, then the right subtree, and on a binary search tree this yields sorted order. Preorder visits the node first, then left, then right. Postorder visits left, then right, then the node last. All three are naturally expressed with recursion and run in linear time.
s1_definition.analogy: Picture auditing the branch hierarchy at the National Bank of India. If you want a sorted roster, you use inorder — handle the junior side first, then the person, then the other side. If you want to copy the whole org chart top-down, you use preorder — write the boss first, then the people under them. If you want to shut down the branch safely, you use postorder — close every subordinate's desk first, and only then close the manager's desk. The order you touch people in depends on the task.
s1_definition.oneliner: Inorder is left-node-right, preorder is node-left-right, postorder is left-right-node.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Traversing a binary tree means visiting every node exactly once in a defined order. The three depth-first traversals differ only in when the current node is visited relative to its subtrees. Inorder visits the left subtree, then the node, then the right subtree, and on a binary search tree this yields sorted order. Preorder visits the node first, then left, then right. Postorder visits left, then right, then the node last. All three are naturally expressed with recursion and run in linear time.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Picture auditing the branch hierarchy at the National Bank of India. If you want a sorted roster, you use inorder — handle the junior side first, then the person, then the other side. If you want to copy the whole org chart top-down, you use preorder — write the boss first, then the people under them. If you want to shut down the branch safely, you use postorder — close every subordinate's desk first, and only then close the manager's desk. The order you touch people in depends on the task.

**One line to remember:** Inorder is left-node-right, preorder is node-left-right, postorder is left-right-node.

sections.s2_technical:
All three traversals walk the same tree; the only difference is the position of the visit statement relative to the two recursive calls. This makes them easy to remember as variations of one template.

Inorder is `inorder(node.left); visit(node); inorder(node.right);`. On a binary search tree this produces ascending sorted output, which is why inorder is the go-to for printing ordered data. Preorder is `visit(node); preorder(node.left); preorder(node.right);`. Because the root is emitted first, preorder is used to serialise or clone a tree, since replaying a preorder rebuilds the same shape. Postorder is `postorder(node.left); postorder(node.right); visit(node);`. Because children are handled before the parent, postorder is used to free or delete a tree safely and to evaluate expression trees where operands must be computed before the operator.

There is also level-order, or breadth-first, traversal, which visits the tree one level at a time using a queue: enqueue the root, then repeatedly dequeue a node, visit it, and enqueue its children. This is used to print a tree by depth or to find the shortest path in an unweighted structure.

A senior-level point is that deep recursion can overflow the call stack, so the iterative versions using an explicit stack, or Morris traversal which uses no extra space by temporarily rewiring pointers, matter for very deep or memory-constrained scenarios. The key insight interviewers look for is that you understand each order maps to a real use: inorder for sorted output, preorder for copy or serialise, postorder for teardown or evaluation.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India stores its product-approval hierarchy as a binary tree and the audit team needs three different reports from the same tree. First, a sorted roster of approvers, which inorder provides directly when the tree is ordered. This is the inorder use case.

Problem 2 — Second, the team needs a top-down export of the chart to replicate it in a new branch, writing the manager before the subordinates. That is exactly preorder. Third, when decommissioning a branch, every subordinate node must be closed before its manager, which is exactly postorder. Showing all three on one tree makes the difference concrete.

In our mini-project we build an `ApprovalTree` of string approver names and provide inorder, preorder, and postorder traversals, plus a level-order traversal using a queue. The demo builds one tree and runs all four traversals, logging the visit order for each so the contrast is obvious.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: a tree with root D, left subtree B holding A and C, right subtree F holding E and G.

Step 1: Inorder on D recurses left to B, then B recurses left to A. A has no children, so it visits A, then visits B, then recurses right to C which visits C. The left subtree yields A, B, C.

Step 2: Back at D, inorder visits D, then recurses right to F which yields E, F, G the same way. The full inorder is A, B, C, D, E, F, G, which is sorted.

Step 3: Preorder on D visits D first, then goes into the left subtree visiting B, then A, then C, then the right subtree visiting F, then E, then G. The order is D, B, A, C, F, E, G, with every parent before its children.

Step 4: Postorder on D handles the left subtree first, visiting A, then C, then B, then the right subtree visiting E, then G, then F, and finally D last. The order is A, C, B, E, G, F, D, with every child before its parent.

Step 5: Level-order starts by enqueuing D. It dequeues and visits D, enqueues B and F. It dequeues B, visits it, enqueues A and C. It dequeues F, visits it, enqueues E and G. Then it visits A, C, E, G in turn.

Step 6: The level-order sequence is D, B, F, A, C, E, G, which reads the tree one depth level at a time.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Traversing a binary tree means visiting every node exactly once, and the three depth-first traversals differ only in when I visit the current node relative to its two subtrees. Inorder visits the left subtree, then the node, then the right subtree, and on a binary search tree this gives the values in sorted ascending order. Preorder visits the node first, then left, then right. Postorder visits left, then right, then the node last. There is also level-order, which visits the tree one depth level at a time using a queue.

What I emphasise in an interview is that each order maps to a real use case, not just an academic definition. I reach for inorder when I need sorted output from an ordered tree. I reach for preorder when I need to copy or serialise a tree, because emitting the root first lets me replay it and rebuild the exact shape. I reach for postorder when I need to tear a tree down safely or evaluate an expression tree, because children must be handled before their parent.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I stored the product-approval hierarchy as a tree and the audit team needed three reports from it. Inorder gave a sorted roster of approvers, preorder gave a top-down export to replicate the chart in a new branch, and postorder gave the safe decommissioning order where every subordinate is closed before its manager. The same tree produced all three simply by changing the visit position.

The senior-level nuance I add is about the call stack. All three recursive traversals are linear time, but deep trees can overflow the stack, so I know the iterative versions using an explicit stack, and Morris traversal which uses no extra space by temporarily rewiring pointers. And when I need a breadth-first view, level-order with a queue is the right tool. Showing that I connect each traversal to a concrete purpose is what signals real understanding rather than memorisation.
